DISTATIS: distances and sorting tasks

Source: vignettes/distatis.Rmd
distatis.Rmd

DISTATIS combines several distance matrices on the same objects. For a sorting task, each assessor groups products by perceived similarity. The analysis gives an object map representing the panel’s consensus, a separate assessor map showing agreement between sorts, and partial object maps showing each assessor’s view. Use covstatis() when your inputs are covariance or connectivity matrices; use distatis() when they are distances.

Sorting the beers

Abdi, Valentin, Chollet, and Chrea (2007) report eight beers sorted by ten assessors. The following is Table 1 of their paper. Numbers identify groups within each assessor’s column; the group labels themselves carry no numeric meaning.

partitions <- matrix(c(
  1,4,3,4,1,1,2,2,1,3,
  4,5,2,5,2,3,1,1,4,3,
  3,1,2,3,2,4,3,1,1,2,
  4,2,3,3,1,1,1,2,1,4,
  1,5,3,5,2,1,1,2,1,3,
  2,3,1,1,3,5,4,4,3,1,
  1,4,3,4,1,1,2,2,2,4,
  5,2,4,2,4,2,5,3,4,5
), 8, 10, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(
  c("Affligen", "Budweiser", "Buckler Blonde", "Killian", "St. Landelin",
    "Buckler Highland", "Fruit Defendu", "EKU28"), paste0("A", 1:10)))

distances <- sorting_distances(partitions)
fit <- distatis(distances, ncomp = 4)
#> Warning: `prep()` was deprecated in multivarious 0.3.0.
#> ℹ Please use `fit()` instead.
#> ℹ The prep() function is deprecated. Use fit() for a more standard interface.
#> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the multivarious package.
#>   Please report the issue to the authors.
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
#> generated.
fit
#> DISTATIS: 8 objects, 10 assessors
#> Retained axes: 4 object, 4 assessor
#> Normalization: mfa; compromise quality: 59.8%
round(fit$alpha, 3)
#>  [1] 0.100 0.101 0.109 0.101 0.099 0.116 0.101 0.109 0.074 0.090

sorting_distances() assigns zero to a pair placed in the same group, and one to a pair placed in different groups. It accepts matrices or data frames, including columns with character labels or factors. An all-in-one-group sort has no contrast and is rejected during fitting because its RV similarities are undefined.

Object and assessor maps 

ggplot2::autoplot(fit, type = "objects", labels = TRUE)

Consensus map of the eight beers.

The default normalization divides each assessor’s centered Gram matrix by its largest eigenvalue. DISTATIS then computes RV similarities between those tables, uses the leading RV eigenvector to obtain nonnegative weights summing to one, and eigendecomposes the weighted compromise. High assessor weight means agreement with this panel; it is not an external measure of accuracy.

ggplot2::autoplot(fit, type = "subjects", labels = TRUE)

Assessor principal coordinates in RV space.

Object and assessor maps have different spectra. Their axes need not have the same rank or interpretation. Requesting ncomp = 4 retains at most four positive axes in each map. Axis percentages always use the full inertia, rather than renormalizing the retained axes to 100%.

round(fit$eigenvalues, 3)
#> [1] 0.664 0.490 0.404 0.339 0.228 0.130 0.050 0.000
round(fit$interstructure_eigenvalues, 3)
#>  [1] 5.983 1.405 0.756 0.708 0.531 0.218 0.194 0.146 0.059 0.000
fit$compromise_quality
#> [1] 0.5982768
sum(fit$inertia[1:4])
#> [1] 0.8228512

These reproduce the paper’s eigenvalues and approximately 60% agreement summary. The first four object axes account for 82.285% of the computed inertia. The supplied author manuscript’s prose gives 84%; that figure does not agree with its eigenvalues, so the package reports the computed ratio.

plot_partial_scores(fit, blocks = 1:3)

Partial maps for three assessors, connected to the compromise.

Each partial map contains one point per object. The compromise is their weighted mean, using fit$alpha. These maps describe variation across assessors; their spread is not a confidence region.

weighted_partial <- Reduce(`+`, Map(`*`, fit$partial_scores, fit$alpha))
max(abs(weighted_partial - multivarious::scores(fit)))
#> [1] 1.373901e-15

plot_block_weights(fit) and plot_block_similarity(fit) display the weights and RV matrix. plot_variance(fit) shows the complete object spectrum; plot_variance(fit, axes = "subjects") shows the assessor spectrum.

General distances and squared distances

distatis() accepts a list of dist objects or square numeric matrices, a three-dimensional object-by-object-by-assessor array, or a single distance table. Objects must have the same order and, when supplied, consistent names in every table. Unnamed inputs are aligned by position.

coordinates <- cbind(c(0, 1, 3, 5), c(0, 2, 1, 4))
D <- as.matrix(dist(coordinates))
ordinary <- distatis(D, norm_method = "none", ncomp = 3)
already_squared <- distatis(D^2, squared = TRUE, norm_method = "none", ncomp = 3)
max(abs(ordinary$compromise_full - already_squared$compromise_full))
#> [1] 0

The default is ordinary distances, as produced by R’s dist(). Set squared = TRUE only when the entries are already squared. Binary sorting distances cannot reveal a mistaken squaring convention, so check this setting when using other distances. norm_method = "frobenius" and "none" are also available; RV similarities determine weights under all normalization choices.

Non-Euclidean distances with materially negative Gram eigenvalues are rejected, with the assessor name and negative inertia in the error. No correction is silently applied. The tol argument controls relative numerical tolerances.

Supplementary assessors and reconstruction

Project a new assessor’s distances on the fitted objects using project_distance(). For both the assessor coordinates and object partial maps, use project_subjects(). Neither function changes the fitted compromise.

partial <- project_distance(fit, distances[[1]])
max(abs(partial - fit$partial_scores[[1]]))
#> [1] 0
supplementary <- project_subjects(fit, distances[1:2])
supplementary$scalar_summaries
#>    subject_id rv_coefficient distance_to_compromise distance_to_subspace
#> A1         A1      0.7680306               0.830311            0.8663089
#> A2         A2      0.8055173               1.006663            0.9252491
max(abs(supplementary$subject_scores - fit$subject_scores[1:2, ]))
#> [1] 1.221245e-15

Supplementary distances use the fit’s squared setting unless overridden. The RV summary compares with the full compromise. distance_to_compromise is the Frobenius distance to that full normalized matrix; distance_to_subspace is the residual from the retained object subspace. These are different diagnostics. Projecting new objects would require a separate out-of-sample MDS procedure and is not supported here.

gram <- multivarious::reconstruct(fit)
compromise_distances <- multivarious::reconstruct(fit, what = "distance")
dim(compromise_distances)
#> [1] 8 8

Reconstruction uses retained object components. Distances are in normalized compromise units, rather than any original assessor’s units. Use all positive object components when full reconstruction is required.

project_table_covariate() and project_feature_covariate() project assessor and object covariates into the corresponding maps. Their cosines and regression slopes are uncentered; center covariates yourself if that matches your question. The existing COVSTATIS inference adapters are explicitly unavailable for DISTATIS: their raw-inner-product refits do not implement its RV geometry.

Reference

Abdi, H., Valentin, D., Chollet, S., & Chrea, C. (2007). Analyzing assessors and products in sorting tasks: DISTATIS, theory and applications. Food Quality and Preference, 18, 627-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2006.09.003.
